**Reading map:** Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, *Mathematics for Machine Learning* (2020), §2.2. This is an original lesson using our delivery-operations example—not reproduced textbook content.

## Why the concept matters

We have six orders, each represented by distance and item count. Instead of fitting a separate expression for every order, arrange the features in rows of one matrix. Matrix multiplication then evaluates one candidate model for every order.

## Define the mathematical relationship

$$
X=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\1&2&2\\1&3&1\\\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\1&6&3\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{6\times3},\quad \hat{\boldsymbol y}=X\boldsymbol\beta
$$

The displayed relationship is the main object to analyse. Specify the relevant dimensions, quantities and assumptions before using it. It should be read as a mathematical statement, not merely a programming shorthand.

## Work through an original example

With beta=(3,2,2)^T, the first row predicts 3+2(1)+2(1)=7 minutes; the second predicts 3+2(2)+2(2)=11 minutes. The observed second time is 12, giving residual 1 minute.

## What follows, and what does not

Rows represent observations and columns represent features, including an intercept column of ones. The dimensions must agree: multiplying a 6-by-3 matrix by a 3-vector yields a 6-vector.

## Test your reasoning

What shape does X^T X have? Why can X beta not multiply a 6-element beta?
